en: The stars scattered across the sky,
Trembling toward the qibla;
The cold wind of dawn roared,
And the reed-tops shivered.
Every living creature awoke,
And fledgling larks twittered;
Insects began to stir,
And the sun’s countenance prepared to meet the earth.
Your uncle, old Bakai—
That hero Bakai—
Hero Bakai started awake,
Prayed to the Almighty,
And prepared to give fodder
To the rangy courser.
One tuft of fescue among eighty grasses—
He had the prancing courser
Graze it in great mouthfuls,
And evenly quenched his thirst
At the bubbling spring.
He made Buurul prance,
Rolled him upon the green turf,
And your uncle Bakai, the gray-wolf lion,
Tethered Buurul high.
Scraping him with a currycomb,
They made Buurul a splendid sight
And cleaned away his heavy sweat.
When Bakai looked from the ridge,
The strands of his coat separated one by one;
When he examined him on every side,
The marks of a courser were revealed.
He could race a bird in flight;
The flank-flesh that would yield rump-fat
Had drawn back and lengthened,
Clinging close to the ribs.
His forelegs were short, his body great;
The marks of a thoroughbred appeared:
Mattock hooves and a broad rump,
A courser bred upon spacious land.
Born in sand and raised among rocks,
He had grown apart without seeing a living soul;
He had raced with wild asses,
With Kylkara of Maiden Saikal
And Kongurbai’s Algara—
He had contended with those steeds.
As a three-year-old he was guarded with great care,
With an owl plume fastened upon his head;
Learned Lady Kanykei,
Fearing that someone’s evil eye would strike him,
Had him raised in a dark place,
Without letting anyone know,
Without letting any person perceive it.
Saying his legs would become bronze,
She trained him in ravined ground;
So that he would never shy from a saddle,
She had him drag a lead-rope from a deer.
His back was high and his temper subdued;
He never tired when raced over ridges.
His withers were high and his temper subdued;
He never tired when sent uphill.
Iron hooves and copper forelegs,
A camel-stallion forelock and owl-like feet—
A true kara-baiyr thoroughbred,
Such was the nature of Buurul.
When he reached his fifth year,
They cut his testicles and made him a gelding;
When the wound had healed,
He curved his neck like a stag.
When he came to a ditch a shrub’s height,
He bounded over without hesitation.
Offering a foot-measure of gold and ser,
The khan of Bukhara asked for him;
But he was not given to those who asked.
Far from giving away the thoroughbred,
No ritually unclean person even knew of him.
He curved his neck like an argali;
When a ditch was a rope-length across,
He bounded over it without swerving.
When they learned of his excellence,
Offering tribute of gold and ser,
Khans from every land asked for him.
But he was not given to those who asked;
No cold-hearted stranger
Ever saw your sultan’s Buurul.
When he took on his summer coat,
He looked dark roan, with a low mane;
When he took on his winter coat,
He appeared bright red-roan.
He never flinched when ridden into battle,
Nor suffered when ridden with the baggage train.
He would not tire if ridden for six months;
Until he reached sixty years,
He would not age or loosen his fangs.
Your uncle, old Bakai,
Scraped the ever-ready Buurul
Again and again with the grooming blade,
And wiped the sweat clean
From the rangy courser.
Old Bakai arranged everything neatly
And tethered Buurul
With a long, loose line.
He prepared him to go out scouting,
To turn back the patrol
Of hero Khan Kongurbai,
And reconnoiter the side road
Used by hero Khan Kongurbai.
Breaking ranks amid crossing spears,
Falling to a bullet if death arrived,
Steeping themselves in bloody gore,
Fighting for six months without fleeing,
Dying if fate should come—
And, if the one God granted honor,
Raiding and seizing the livestock
Of the full-strength infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai;
Wreaking spectacular slaughter
Upon the bastard Chinese;
And, as a son, avenging
His lord who had gone to Judgment Day—
With these aims he prepared Buurul.
Starting awake from sleep,
He rolled onto his right side,
Gathered himself like a lion,
And strained like a blue tiger.
Preparing to face Beijing,
The splendid hero, the valiant man’s son,
Prayed to the one God.
Ah, the broad and splendid lion,
The unshakable noble hero,
Rose awake from sleep,
Pondering the affairs of Beijing.
He dipped his hands in water
And performed the ablution of his hands;
He put his feet into the water
And performed the ablution of his feet.
Facing the qibla,
His champion uncle Bakai
Now called the azan in a resounding voice.
He hurriedly performed the prayer,
And saddled the choice thoroughbred,
Hurrying in great agitation,
Putting on Akolpok,
And readying his arms and armor.
Yesterday—have you heard of this?
While bloodthirsty Manas lived,
It was encountered through the unseen,
Found upon the open plain,
And, by God’s decree, came
To Sayypkurush, the hero and lion.
The six-edged blade that fell from the sky,
The finest of all sword blades—
Have you heard of it?
Zulpukor, which remained from Manas.
Zulpukor, left as a gift
By valiant Manas, the gray wolf—
When he attacked the shouting foe,
When he drew it from its sheath
And entered the enemy without looking back,
It would bring the end of days.
Until it had drunk its fill of blood,
It would not return to the sheath when put away;
When swung this way and that,
It never went idle without taking a head.
When grasped in the hand with a shout,
It went wherever it was swung;
When its bearer entered the grappling foe,
It drenched them in bright-red blood.
Zulpukor, inherited as a legacy
From Manas, the gray wolf of old—
That was his treasure when he rode on campaign.
The splendid champion, son of the Bloodthirsty One,
Girded on the sword Zulpukor,
And like a cloud about to rain again,
His face turned wrathful.
He buckled the gray kise left by Manas
Around his slender waist.
The object held in the gray wolf’s hand
When he stood leaning upon it
Was a golden-cheeked battle-axe;
On the gray wolf’s left side
Was a side-pouch made of gold.
The sight arrested the heart;
When one looked upon
The handsome-born champion’s other side,
An okchontoi and quiver could be seen.
On a level upland at a forked pass,
Upon a ridge no horse could cross,
He gathered himself in anger;
The splendid hero, son of the Bloodthirsty One,
Leaned upon Akkelte.
Though he had come to spread alarm,
The splendid hero, son of Manas—
That broad and noble hero—
Was not yet one to stir.
The surpassing lion, son of Manas,
Arrested the heart when seen;
He appeared to have been born surpassing
His father Manas, the gray wolf.
Upon a divided pass and open plain,
Beside a black rock like a yurt,
Atop the black rock,
Crouching like a blue tiger,
He faced toward Beijing.
Without taking its strap around his neck,
The immeasurable spyglass
He drew from his breast:
A broad spyglass with an adzelike mouth,
A great spyglass a full fathom long,
Its inside glowing red like fire,
The great spyglass left by the bloodthirsty hero.
When he drew it from its case,
It extended a full fathom.
When bloodthirsty lion Manas
Trampled down
The whole world,
When he alone knew
And held dominion over
Much of the face of the earth,
When he humiliated the khoja in Kokon,
When he destroyed
The afflicted one in Bukhara,
When he brought turmoil
Upon all who challenged him,
When he seized those
Who defied him
And struck them down
Upon the steppe,
When he made broad Talas his fortress
And guarded it,
When he crushed whoever he encountered
And consumed them,
Yesterday, Azhybai and Khan Bakai were there,
And Almambet and Chubak were there too;
All the lions were there.
Yesterday, loading ammunition on an elephant,
Taking the warriors together,
All the heroes gathered.
They found no mountain difficult enough to cross,
And no enemy to fight.
Beyond Andizhan,
On this side of Namangan,
In the shelter of the Kokon khan,
Upon a yellow plain like the moon,
Dragging their wagons,
Leading a bay mare without a saddle,
Sixty Russian surveyors
Came out.
Sword in hand and shouting,
Mighty Alman then
Attacked them with a clamor
And took it as plunder.
The great spyglass taken as booty
Had its handle wound in gold.
Its maker was a friend of David;
When news came from your prince,
The hunchbacked smith Bölökbai
Repaired it, poor man.
